701.title: Nanak on the mountain
701.hook: Bhai Gurdas tells of the yogis on Mount Sumer asking Nanak about the world below (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
701.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's meetings with the siddhs, told by Bhai Gurdas and in the Siddh Gosht of the Guru Granth Sahib, as a call to live a holy life within the world rather than withdrawing from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharamsal: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, the mist cleared, and homes filled with song. Today the light goes climbing.

So, how are things down there? It's what you ask someone who's just come in from outside. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, it's asked on a mountain. Guru Nanak climbs up to Sumer, and the siddhs are there, yogis who have left the world far below them to practice in the heights. They see him arrive, and they ask him for news. Year one told what Nanak said to yogis about living in the world. Today, Bhai Gurdas's version of the question, and the answer he remembers. Today: siddhs.
screen: `SO, HOW ARE THINGS DOWN THERE?` → `THE SIDDHS ON SUMER.` → `NANAK ON THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the siddhs ask Nanak what's happening in the world of mortals, the world below. A polite question, maybe a curious one. Nanak's answer is not small talk. He says truth has become like a moon that can't be seen, and falsehood like a moonless dark. He says he has gone out searching through that dark. Then he turns the question around. The siddhs, he says, have gone and hidden in the mountains. So who is going to carry the world across? There's an edge to that. The yogis asked about the world below as if it were somebody else's problem, interesting news from far away. Nanak answers as if they're part of the story: the people best trained in stillness and discipline have climbed out of reach, just when the world needs them. Bhai Gurdas is not mocking the siddhs' discipline. He takes it seriously, which is why the question bites. Training means something because of what it's for. Holiness, in this telling, doesn't belong up on the mountain looking down. It belongs back in the valley, with the farmers, the traders, the families, the people living in the dark. Which is where Nanak himself is going: tomorrow to Mecca, and soon, home to Kartarpur. The mountain is a place to visit. The world below is where the work is.
screen: `WHAT'S HAPPENING IN THE WORLD BELOW?` · `TRUTH LIKE A HIDDEN MOON.` · `WHO WILL CARRY THE WORLD ACROSS?` · `THE WORK IS IN THE VALLEY.` · then, large: `WHAT OF THE WORLD BELOW.`

segments.voice: Stand somewhere a little high, the top of a staircase, an upstairs window, even the step outside your door, and look down at the street and the people passing. Ask the siddhs' question honestly, what is happening down there, who is struggling, and let one face or one place come to mind. If you pray, you can hold that person in the Name for a while.
Siddhs, yogis who climbed Sumer to leave the world below, asking Nanak for its news, and hearing him ask back who would carry that world across.
Your line: what of the world below. Nanak's answer was to go back down. Until tomorrow.

702.title: Mecca, in the Vars
702.hook: Bhai Gurdas tells how Nanak answered the qazis that deeds, not labels, count (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
702.howItsDone: Sikhs retell Guru Nanak's answer at Mecca, as Bhai Gurdas gives it, as a teaching that good deeds, not religious labels, count before God, and they apply it to themselves as much as to anyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, siddhs, the yogis on Sumer, and Nanak's question back to them: who will carry the world below across? Today, a city of pilgrims.

Open your book, and tell us. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, that's the demand put to Guru Nanak at Mecca. A traveler in blue clothes, with a staff in his hand and a book under his arm, has arrived among the pilgrims. Year one told one story from that visit: the traveler asleep with his feet toward the Kaaba. Today, Bhai Gurdas's next stanza, and the question that came after. Today's word: Mecca.
screen: `OPEN YOUR BOOK AND TELL US.` → `A TRAVELER IN BLUE, WITH A BOOK.` → `THE QUESTION AFTER.`

segments.voice: In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the qazis and mullahs gather around Nanak with the question of the age you heard about three days ago. Open your book, they say, and tell us: who is greater, the Hindu or the Muslim? It's a trap shaped like a quiz. Pick one, and you've joined the quarrel. Refuse, and you look evasive. Bhai Gurdas says Nanak answered the pilgrims plainly: without good deeds, both will weep. Neither the Hindu nor the Muslim, by the label alone, finds shelter at God's court. Then he reaches for a picture from the dyer's yard. Safflower gives cloth a bright color, but it's a raw color. Wash it, and it runs out. A label, Bhai Gurdas suggests, is like that dye: bright on the surface, gone in the first wash. What holds is what's done. Look at what Nanak doesn't do here. He doesn't say both are wrong, or both are right, or that some third thing is better. He moves the question off the label and onto the life. Deeds; amal is the word Bhai Gurdas uses. And he names the real problem in the same stanza: people quarrel with each other while Ram and Rahim are one. For Sikhs, the weight of this answer is that it falls on everyone equally. A Sikh who leans on the label of being a Sikh is wearing the same safflower dye. The book Nanak opens, in this telling, doesn't announce a winner. It asks what you did.
screen: `WHO IS GREATER, HINDU OR MUSLIM?` · `WITHOUT GOOD DEEDS, BOTH WILL WEEP.` · `SAFFLOWER DYE: GONE IN THE WASH.` · `THE ANSWER FALLS ON EVERYONE.` · then, large: `DEEDS, NOT LABELS.`

segments.voice: Choose one good deed nobody will trace back to you: paying for the next person's coffee, wiping down the shared table at work, picking up the litter on your own street. Decide what it will be, then let it go, with no post and no telling anyone, not even later. If you pray, you can offer the deed quietly in the Name.
Mecca, in the vars. In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the place where Nanak was asked who is greater, and answered that without good deeds, both will weep.
Your line: deeds, not labels. A book opened, and no winner announced. Day seven hundred two, done.

703.title: Nanak at Baghdad
703.hook: Nanak and Mardana at Baghdad, where he speaks of worlds beyond worlds (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
703.howItsDone: Sikhs retell Guru Nanak's visit to Baghdad from Bhai Gurdas's first var, and connect his words there to the Japji's teaching that creation has no limit anyone can count.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mecca, where Nanak answered that without good deeds, both will weep. Today the road reaches a great city.

Two travelers have stopped at a great city. One is Baba Nanak. The other carries a rebab, a stringed instrument, and his name is Mardana. The city is Baghdad, and the var puts their camp outside it, beyond the walls. Bhai Gurdas sets the scene in a single line: here is Baba, and here is Mardana, the rebab player. Then something happens that makes everything go quiet. Today: karah prashad.
screen: `CAMP OUTSIDE A GREAT CITY.` → `BABA, AND MARDANA WITH HIS REBAB.` → `EVERYTHING GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak gave a call, and the world around fell silent, as if in a trance. A holy man of the city, a pir, came to see who this faqir was. And in the talk that followed, Nanak spoke of what lies beyond the edges of the known world: skies beyond skies, and worlds below worlds, past anyone's counting. The pir asked to be shown. In Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak took the pir's son with him, and in the blink of an eye showed him those worlds, and they came back carrying a bowl of karah prashad, the sweet offering, from a world below. You can hold that last part however your tradition holds it. Some readers take it as it's told. Others hear it as a picture. Either way, the story is about size. If you learned the Japji in year one, you've heard this in the Guru's own words. In the twenty-second pauri, Guru Nanak says there are nether worlds below nether worlds, and skies above skies. People have tried to find the limit, and they can't. If it could be written down, someone would write it, but the writing would run out first. The pir's world had edges. Nanak's answer took the edges away, not to make anyone feel small, but to make God large: whatever you've counted, the Creator is beyond it. And notice who is in the scene's first line: Baba, and Mardana, the rebab player. Even a story about countless worlds starts with a musician sitting beside his friend outside the walls.
screen: `A CALL, AND THE CITY FALLS SILENT.` · `SKIES BEYOND SKIES, WORLDS BELOW WORLDS.` · `THE JAPJI, PAURI 22: PAST COUNTING.` · `STILL, THE FRIEND AT YOUR SIDE.` · then, large: `WORLDS BEYOND WORLDS.`

segments.voice: If it's dark, look up at the night sky from a door or a window, find the farthest light you can see, and remember that it's not the edge; if it's daytime, close your eyes and picture the sky over your roof at midnight. Let your breath slow down under all that size; you don't have to understand any of it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, wonder, to the dark.
Karah prashad, the sweet offering Nanak and the pir's son brought back from a world below, in Bhai Gurdas's telling of worlds beyond counting.
Your line: worlds beyond worlds. The writing runs out before the wonder does. See you tomorrow.

704.title: Home in ordinary clothes
704.hook: back at Kartarpur, Nanak lays down the pilgrim's robe and lives as a householder (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
704.howItsDone: Sikhs live as householders rather than renunciants, working, raising families and keeping the daily banis at home, and they point to Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur as the pattern.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karah prashad, and worlds beyond worlds, past anyone's counting. Today the traveler comes home.

The suitcase goes down in the hall. The shoes come off. The clothes that smell of trains and other people's cities go into the wash, and you pull on the soft old things you only wear at home. There's a particular relief in that moment: the trip is over, and ordinary life can start again. Bhai Gurdas gives Guru Nanak that moment too, after the mountain, Mecca and Baghdad. Today: udasi.
screen: `THE SUITCASE IN THE HALL.` → `TRAVEL CLOTHES OFF.` → `ORDINARY LIFE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says: then Baba came to Kartarpur, and took off the whole garb of the udasi, the wandering renunciant. He put on the clothes of a householder, worldly clothes, and sat on a manji, a simple cot, and taught from there. Year one told you about the farmer at Kartarpur, working the land by the river. Today, look at the clothes. On the road, Nanak wore the wanderer's garb. At home, he takes it off, and nothing about him says holy man to a passerby. He looks like anyone in the village. Bhai Gurdas doesn't treat this as a step down. He tells it as the point. The holiness didn't live in the robe, so taking the robe off costs nothing. Then he tells what daily life at Kartarpur sounded like. The Guru's word was spoken there, he says, and light spread and darkness went. Sodar and Aarti, the evening hymns, were sung, and the Japji was recited at amritvela, the early hours before dawn. That's the shape of the day you learned all last year: the Japji before sunrise, the evening prayers at dusk. In Bhai Gurdas's telling, it's already there at Kartarpur, kept by a man in ordinary clothes, in an ordinary village, between the farming and the meals. Holiness came home, and it looked like a routine.

segments.voice: Choose one small task right in front of you, washing a cup, folding a shirt, watering a plant, and do it slowly, with your full attention, as if it were the most important thing in the house, because for these few minutes it is. No special clothes, no special place; if you pray, you can let Waheguru ride along with each movement.

705.title: The debate at Achal
705.hook: at Achal Batala the yogis test Nanak with miracles; he says his only miracle is the true Name (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
705.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's answer at Achal, as Bhai Gurdas tells it, as a teaching that the Name, not wonder-working, is the heart of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, udasi: Nanak set aside the wanderer's garb and was holy in ordinary clothes. Today, a crowd notices him.

A fair is a noisy place: stalls, crowds, music, smoke from cooking fires, people who've walked all day to be there. Bhai Gurdas tells of one at Achal, near Batala, for Shivratri, a festival of Shiva, with yogis gathered there. Baba Nanak came, and the whole crowd turned to see him. The yogis did not take it well, and Bhai Gurdas tells what followed without softening it. Today: Achal.
screen: `A FAIR AT ACHAL, ON SHIVRATRI.` → `THE CROWD TURNS TO NANAK.` → `THE YOGIS DON'T TAKE IT WELL.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says the yogis burned with jealousy when they saw it. The debate starts sharp. A yogi named Bhangar Nath goes after the very thing you heard about yesterday. You were a wanderer, he says, and now you've gone back to a householder's life. Isn't that spoiling the milk? Nanak's answer turns it around: you left home behind, and yet you go begging at householders' doors. Then the yogis try a different kind of argument. Bhai Gurdas describes them showing off their powers, taking strange shapes, doing marvels, and then turning to Nanak. Show us something, they say. The whole world has seen what you can do. Show us a miracle too. Here is the line at the center of today. Nanak answers that apart from the true Name, he has no other miracle. In the same exchange he says there's no other support for him but the Guru's company and the Guru's word. Notice what he's refusing: to make holiness a contest of who can astonish whom. A miracle performed to win an argument is a show, and a show is about the performer. The Name points away from the performer, toward the One. Bhai Gurdas sets that one plain sentence against all the yogis' marvels.
screen: `SPOILING THE MILK?` · `SHOW US A MIRACLE.` · `NO MIRACLE BUT THE TRUE NAME.` · `HOLINESS IS NOT A CONTEST.` · then, large: `THE ONLY MIRACLE.`

segments.voice: Picture a moment coming today when you could be impressive, mentioning the thing you did, topping someone's story with a bigger one, being the cleverest voice in the room, and then picture letting it pass: not hiding anything, just not performing. Notice how the urge feels in your body and let it settle; if you pray, you can say the Name quietly in the place where the show would have been.
Achal, the fair near Batala where yogis demanded a miracle, and Nanak said that apart from the true Name, he had none.
Your line: the only miracle. One plain sentence, set against all the marvels. Until tomorrow.

706.title: Milk and jasmine at Multan
706.hook: tradition says Multan's holy men sent a brimming cup of milk; Nanak floated a jasmine flower on it
706.tomorrow: The Guru bows to the disciple
706.howItsDone: Sikhs retell the story of the milk and the jasmine at Multan as a picture of humility: entering a full place gently, adding fragrance without pushing anyone aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Achal, where Nanak said the true Name was his only miracle. Today, an answer with no words at all.

A cup filled to the very brim, carried across a courtyard by someone walking slowly, not daring to breathe. Bhai Gurdas records no words with it. The cup itself is the message. He tells this at Multan. When Baba Nanak arrived, the pirs of Multan, its holy men, came to him with a cup brimming with milk. And Nanak answered with no words either. Today: Multan.
screen: `A CUP FILLED TO THE BRIM.` → `THE CUP IS THE MESSAGE.` → `AN ANSWER WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the cup. Sikhs read it as the pirs' polite, pointed message: this city is already full of holy men. There's no room for another. Like milk to the brim, one more drop and it spills. Now the answer. Bhai Gurdas says Baba took a jasmine flower and put it in the milk. That's all. In the telling Sikhs pass on, not a drop spills, and the milk now carries a scent it didn't have before. The reply does several things at once. It agrees: yes, the cup is full. It doesn't argue that there's room, or push anyone aside. It doesn't spill the milk, which would have been an insult to the pirs and their city. And it shows that something light enough, gentle enough, can still be added to a full place without taking anything from it. It also speaks the pirs' own language. They said it with a cup, and Nanak answered the same way, courteously, and still said what he came to say. Bhai Gurdas closes the scene with a picture of his own: it was like the Ganges merging into the ocean. A great river doesn't make the sea overflow. It comes in, and becomes part of it. Hear that the way Bhai Gurdas tells it, not as a victory over the holy men of Multan, but as a meeting where nothing was lost.

707.title: The Guru bows to the disciple
707.hook: Bhai Gurdas marvels that Nanak bowed to Angad, making the disciple the Guru (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)
707.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's handing on to Guru Angad, as Bhai Gurdas tells it, as one light passing into a new form, and today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Multan: a full cup, and a jasmine flower that spilled nothing. Today, a handover that runs the other way.

A handover at work tends to go one way. The old boss signs the papers, gives a short speech, maybe cuts a cake, and walks out the door, and the new one is still, somehow, the junior. Near the end of his first var, Bhai Gurdas tells a handover that runs the other way round. Baba Nanak chooses the one who will carry the light after him, and then does something that makes Bhai Gurdas marvel. Today: Angad.
screen: `A HANDOVER, THE USUAL WAY.` → `BABA NANAK CHOOSES WHO COMES NEXT.` → `A HANDOVER THE OTHER WAY ROUND.`

segments.voice: The disciple's name was Lehna. Bhai Gurdas says that while Nanak was still living, he set Lehna in the Guru's place and had the canopy held over his head, the sign of the Guru's seat. He gave him a new name, Angad. And Bhai Gurdas treats it as a wonder: the master bowing to the one he'd chosen. The bow is sung in the Guru Granth Sahib too, in the var of Satta and Balwand on Ang nine hundred sixty-six: the Guru bowed to the disciple while Nanak was still alive. Bhai Gurdas pictures it as light merging into light. Nanak's light didn't go out. It wasn't handed along like a lamp passed from one hand to another, leaving the first hand empty. It merged: the same light, now in a new form. Sikhs often sum it up in a phrase that turns the order upside down: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru. In Sikh teaching, Guruship isn't a possession to clutch until the end. It's a light, and the one who carries it is the first to bow to it when it shines in someone else. Bhai Gurdas goes on to tell the next handings on in the same spirit, and the pattern carries into Sikh life now, where Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru. Bowing to someone you taught means trusting that what you gave them is theirs now, and might grow in their hands in ways it never could in yours. Nanak, in Bhai Gurdas's telling, does it with the Guru's own seat.
